sections.h: Baal of Peor and the harvest gods (Hosea 9)
sections.b: Hosea 9 names two meetings with Baal. The earlier is at Peor in Moab, where Israel "tied itself" to the local Baal (Numbers 25:3). The later is at every threshing floor, where the grain is received as "a prostitute's pay", a gift from the god of rain and storm. The chapter calls Baal "the Shameful Thing", as Jeremiah does (Jeremiah 3:24; 11:13).

sections.h: Hosea: Gibeah as a byword
sections.b: Hosea names Gibeah three times (5:8; 9:9; 10:9). In 9:9 and 10:9 "the days of Gibeah" mean the crime of Judges 19 and its aftermath, the standard for how low Israel can sink. A second reading links the phrase to Saul's Gibeah and the demand for a king.

sections.h: Hosea's Gilgal
sections.b: For Hosea Gilgal is a shrine of the northern kingdom and the place where the LORD says "there I came to hate them" (9:15). He names it with Bethel as a place the people should not go to (4:15), and calls its altars heaps of stones (12:11). A suggested link with Saul's kingship at Gilgal (1 Samuel 11:15) is debated.

sections.h: Hosea: Egypt and Assyria as the places of exile
sections.b: Hosea 8:13; 9:3, 6; 11:5 and 11:11 name Egypt and Assyria together as the places Israel is sent. Egypt is the old house of bondage, Assyria the new one. Hosea 9:3 adds that in exile they will eat unclean food, a worry repeated by Ezekiel (4:13) and Daniel (1:8).

sections.h: Hosea: the luxuriant vine
sections.b: Hosea 10:1 calls Israel a boqeq vine, "luxuriant" in the Plain English Translation, though the Hebrew can also mean "empty" or "plundering". It bore fruit for itself, and the fruit turned to altars. In 14:7 the picture comes back reversed: those who live in the LORD's shade "will blossom like the vine".

sections.h: Hosea 14: the vine and the cypress
sections.b: After the luxuriant vine of 10:1 that bore fruit for itself, the last chapter promises that those who live in the LORD's shade will "blossom like the vine", with fame like the wine of Lebanon (14:7), and the LORD is a cypress from which comes Ephraim's fruit (14:8).

sections.h: Hosea: pillars beside the altars
sections.b: Hosea names pillars (matsevot) with altars as a mark of the Baal cult: the richer the land, the finer the pillars (10:1), and the LORD will wreck them (10:2). In 3:4 "no pillar" is a loss, in a list of things that go with kings, sacrifice and ephod.

sections.h: Hosea: Bethel as Beth-aven
sections.b: Hosea twists "Bethel", house of God, into "Beth-aven", house of wickedness (4:15; 5:8; 10:5). In 10:15 he names Bethel itself: "This is what Bethel has done to you." In 12:4 it is the place where Jacob met God and God spoke with "us", making Bethel the place where the people's story began and the place where they went wrong.

sections.h: Hosea: the calf of Samaria
sections.b: Hosea is the only prophet to speak of the calf in Samaria (8:5-6), the "heifers of Beth-aven" (10:5) and kissing calves (13:2). He denies the defense that the calf was only a pedestal: "A craftsman made it, and it is no god" (8:6). It will turn to splinters and be carried to Assyria as tribute (10:6).
sections.refs: Hosea 8:5; Hosea 8:6; Hosea 10:5; Hosea 10:6; Hosea 13:2; 1 Kings 12:28-30

sections.h: Hosea: buying help from Assyria
sections.b: Hosea speaks of Ephraim going "up to Assyria" and hiring lovers (8:9), of a calf carried there as a gift to King Jareb (10:6) and of Assyria as the king of a people who refused to turn back (11:5). The background is in 2 Kings 15:19-20; 16:7-10; 17:3-6.
sections.refs: Hosea 8:9; Hosea 8:10; Hosea 10:6; Hosea 11:5; 2 Kings 15:19; 2 Kings 17:3

sections.h: Hosea 11:1 and Matthew 2:15
sections.b: Matthew quotes "Out of Egypt I called my son" for Jesus' return from Egypt. In Hosea the line is about the Exodus, in the LORD's recollection of Israel as a young son. Most students call Matthew's use typology: Israel's story is a pattern Jesus repeats as the true Son. The Hebrew has "my son"; the Greek of Hosea has "his children", and Matthew follows the Hebrew.

sections.h: Hosea 11:8-9: the heart that turns over
sections.b: The LORD says "My heart turns over inside me, and all my pity grows warm" and then "I am God, not a human being" (11:8-9). The verb "turns over" is the one used of the overthrow of Sodom; the root of "pity" is the root of "relent". The passage is the central text for the question whether God feels and whether his "not changing" excludes feeling. Compare Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29, which use the same words "not a human being".
sections.refs: Hosea 11:8; Hosea 11:9; Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:29; Genesis 19:25; Jeremiah 31:20

sections.h: Hosea: the Exodus told as a parent's memory
sections.b: Hosea 11:1-4 retells the Exodus and the wilderness as a parent's story: calling, teaching to walk, healing, easing the yoke, feeding. Hosea 12:9, 13 and 13:4-5 also recall Egypt, the prophet who led Israel out, and the wilderness. The reversal "back to Egypt" (8:13; 9:3) and the return "like a bird as they come out of Egypt" (11:11) use the same pattern in both directions.
sections.refs: Hosea 11:1-4; Hosea 12:9; Hosea 12:13; Hosea 13:4-5; Hosea 8:13; Hosea 11:11

sections.h: Hosea 11:1: Israel as the LORD's son
sections.b: "When Israel was a youth, I loved him, and I called my son out of Egypt." The family language comes from Exodus 4:22, where Israel is "my son, my firstborn", and it is carried on in Jeremiah 31:9, where Ephraim is "my firstborn". Matthew applies Hosea's line to Jesus (Matthew 2:15).

sections.h: Hosea 12: Jacob as pattern and warning
sections.b: Hosea 12:2-6, 12-13 tells three scenes of Jacob's life: the heel-grabbing in the womb (Genesis 25:26), the struggle with the angel, and Bethel. Here Jacob is treated as a model for his descendants, and scholars differ on whether it is condemnation, example, or both. The flight to Aram and the service for a wife are set against the LORD's keeping of Israel by a prophet.
sections.refs: Hosea 12:2; Hosea 12:3; Hosea 12:4; Hosea 12:12; Genesis 25:26; Genesis 32:28

common: Jacob in Hosea 12 is a positive model of persistence and prayer.
uncommon: Jacob in Hosea 12 is entirely negative, a list of faults.

sections.h: Hosea 12: the prophet who led Israel out
sections.b: Hosea 12:13 says that "by a prophet the LORD brought Israel up out of Egypt, and by a prophet he was watched over". Moses is not named. The sentence stands beside 12:10 (the LORD spoke to the prophets and gave visions) and 9:7-8 (the prophet called a fool).

sections.h: Hosea 12:7-8: rigged scales and a rich man's innocence
sections.b: Hosea calls Ephraim "Canaan" with scales of deceit and has him say "I have become rich ... No one will find ... any guilt in me". The picture is of wealth used as proof of virtue. Ezekiel, Amos and Revelation 3:17 have close parallels.

sections.h: Hosea: treaties with Assyria and gifts to Egypt
sections.b: Hosea speaks of a covenant with Assyria and oil sent to Egypt (12:1), of Ephraim as a silly dove calling to Egypt and Assyria (7:11) and of lovers hired among the nations (8:9). The last king, Hoshea, tried both (2 Kings 17:3-4).

sections.h: Hosea 12:9: tents as on festival days
sections.b: "Again I will settle you in tents, as on festival days." The line recalls the feast of Booths and the wilderness years, and can be read as a threat of exile, a promise of restoration or a memory of the feast. It stands in the book beside the autumn festival of 9:5.

sections.h: Hosea 13:14: 'Where are your plagues, Death?'
sections.b: Hosea 13:14 asks whether the LORD will ransom people from Sheol and redeem them from death, and then calls on Death and Sheol with the words "Where are your plagues, Death? Where is your destruction, Sheol?" The Hebrew has no mark of question or statement, so the lines may be a threat or a promise. Paul takes up the second pair of questions in 1 Corinthians 15:55. The nearby verse 6:2 ("On the third day he will raise us up") is the other Hosea text read with the resurrection.

common: Hosea 13:14 is a promise that Paul quotes in 1 Corinthians 15:55.
uncommon: Hosea 13:14 is a threat in its own setting, which Paul reverses.

sections.h: Hosea 13:14: Sheol and Death called by name
sections.b: In Hosea 13:14 Sheol and Death are addressed like persons: "Where are your plagues, Death? Where is your destruction, Sheol?" The LORD asks whether he should take people from "the hand of Sheol", an expression that Psalm 49:15 uses as a believer's hope. In the Greek Sheol is Hades, and Paul's second "Death" became "Hades" in later manuscripts.

sections.h: Hosea on kings: made without the LORD, given in anger
sections.b: Hosea speaks of kings made by murder (8:4), of the people who say "We have no king" (10:3) and of the king "given in anger" and "taken away in fury" (13:10-11). He quotes the request of 1 Samuel 8:5. Whether he opposes monarchy as such or only the northern usurpers is debated, since 3:5 looks to "David their king".
sections.refs: Hosea 3:5; Hosea 8:4; Hosea 10:3; Hosea 13:10; Hosea 13:11; 1 Samuel 8:5

sections.h: Hosea: the fall of Samaria told plainly
sections.b: Hosea 13:16 describes the fall of Samaria as war was fought: the sword, the smashing of children, the splitting open of pregnant women. 10:7 says Samaria's king will be like a twig on water, and 10:14 recalls an earlier atrocity. The sack of 722 BC is told in 2 Kings 17:5-6.

sections.h: Hosea 14: the words to bring
sections.b: Hosea 14:1-3 is the book's fullest call to repentance and its model prayer: turn back; bring words; ask for forgiveness; pledge the offering of lips; give up Assyria, horses and homemade gods. The LORD answers, "I will heal their turning away" (14:4). The shuv of the call is also in 6:1, 11:5 and 12:6, and the LORD's own "I will not come back to wreck Ephraim" in 11:9.
sections.refs: Hosea 6:1; Hosea 11:5; Hosea 12:6; Hosea 14:1; Hosea 14:2; Hosea 14:4

sections.h: Hosea 14:2-4: forgive and heal
sections.b: The people are told to ask: "Forgive all our guilt and accept what is good." The LORD's answer goes beyond forgiveness: "I will heal their turning away. I will love them freely." In Jeremiah 3:22 the same promise is given in the same words.

sections.h: Hosea on sacrifice: gifts that please no one, and the bulls of the lips
sections.b: Hosea says that Ephraim built "altar after altar for sin" (8:11), and that the sacrifices they eat as meat do not please the LORD (8:13); in exile there will be none to offer (9:4). At the end of the book the returning people offer "the bulls of our lips" (14:2), words in place of animals; Hebrews 13:15 follows the Greek, "the fruit of lips". Hosea 6:6 states the principle.
sections.refs: Hosea 6:6; Hosea 8:11; Hosea 8:13; Hosea 9:4; Hosea 14:2; Hebrews 13:15

sections.h: Hosea: love withdrawn and love given freely
sections.b: The LORD says "I will love them no more" (9:15) and then, in the last chapter, "I will love them freely" (14:4). Between lie the parent's love of 11:1-4 and the turning of his heart in 11:8. "Sow for yourselves in righteousness; reap by the measure of loyal love" (10:12) and "Keep loyal love and justice" (12:6) are the demand on Israel.
sections.refs: Hosea 9:15; Hosea 10:12; Hosea 11:1; Hosea 11:8; Hosea 12:6; Hosea 14:4

sections.h: Hosea on idols: made by hand, kissed, given up
sections.b: Hosea ridicules the images: "A craftsman made it, and it is no god" (8:6); idols "formed with their own skill, every one the work of a craftsman" (13:2); the pledge to stop calling the work of their hands 'Our gods' (14:3). In 14:8 the LORD says "Ephraim, what more do I have to do with idols?".

sections.h: Hosea: back to Egypt, out of Egypt
sections.b: Egypt in Hosea is the place of the Exodus (11:1; 12:9, 13; 13:4), the place of refuge and the place of the new exile (8:13; 9:3, 6; 11:5), a partner in treaties (12:1), and the place from which the children will come "like birds" (11:11). Matthew 2:15 takes up 11:1.
sections.refs: Hosea 8:13; Hosea 9:3; Hosea 9:6; Hosea 11:1; Hosea 11:5; Hosea 11:11; Hosea 12:9; Hosea 12:13; Matthew 2:15

sections.h: Hosea: the return of the children
sections.b: Hosea speaks of the return from Egypt and Assyria, "like a bird" and "like a dove" (11:10-11), and of those who live in the LORD's shade returning (14:7). Paul reads Hosea beside the "remnant" in Romans 9:25-27.

sections.h: Hosea 8-14: the last chapters of the book
sections.b: The second half of Hosea moves from the alarm and the calf (8), the harvest and the days of Gibeah (9), the luxuriant vine (10), the parent's love (11), Jacob and Ephraim (12), the lion and Death (13), to the call to turn back and the closing note for the wise reader (14). Numbering: English 11:12, 13:16 and 14:1-9 are Hebrew 12:1, 14:1 and 14:2-10, and English 12:1-14 is Hebrew 12:2-15.
